Neonatal harp seals (Pagophilus groenlandicus) emerge from the womb at a body length of approximately 85 centimeters [Lb = approximately 85 centimeters], a dimension that facilitates rapid movement through the unstable pack ice during the vulnerable first days of life. Newborns carry a substantial wet weight of about 10,000 grams [Wwb = about 10,000 grams] at birth, a mass composed largely of brown adipose tissue and maternally derived fluids that provide essential thermal insulation against the subzero environment. This substantial birth mass is critical for survival in the harsh Arctic climate where pups must quickly accumulate blubber reserves. Field observations consistently confirm this neonatal length across the major breeding grounds in the Northwest Atlantic and the Greenland Sea, with negligible variation between populations. The characteristic white lanugo coat, which is shed after several weeks, does not affect the basic somatic dimensions recorded at parturition. Comparative data from related phocid species suggest that a neonatal length near 85 cm is typical for ice-breeding seals, though the precise value varies with maternal body condition and local environmental conditions at the time of delivery.

Harp seal mothers nurse their pups on the ice for a remarkably brief period. The time elapsed since birth at weaning is only 12 days [tx = 12 days], one of the shortest lactation durations among any mammalian species adapted to high latitudes at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This truncated nursing interval, occurring under the thermal conditions of the mother's core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], forces the pup to gain weight at an extraordinary rate. By the time maternal provisioning ceases, the pup has increased its body mass substantially, achieving a wet weight at weaning of approximately 35,000 grams [Wwx = approximately 35,000 grams]. This represents a tripling of birth mass in less than two weeks, an accretion rate fueled by the exceptionally lipid-rich milk of harp seals, which may contain over 50 percent fat. The rapid weaning is an adaptive response to the instability of the ice platform; a longer nursing period would expose pups to the risk of being separated from their mothers by shifting ice floes or early breakup. After weaning, juveniles must rapidly learn to forage independently.

The reproductive physiology of the harp seal is characterized by a complex gestational timeline. Females exhibit a total gestation time of 348 days [tg = 348 days], calculated from conception to parturition, though this figure encompasses a substantial period of embryonic diapause at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The active gestation phase comprises approximately 228 days following a 120-day period of delayed implantation, during which the fertilized blastocyst remains quiescent in the uterine tract. This reproductive strategy, occurring at a maternal core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], ensures that parturition is synchronized with the annual formation of stable pack ice in late February and March. The delayed implantation mechanism allows mothers to time birth so that the brief, intensive lactation period coincides with optimal ice conditions and adequate maternal energy reserves accumulated during summer foraging. Approximately 228 days of true gestation follow implantation, during which organogenesis and rapid foetal growth proceed. The total duration from copulation to birth thus spans nearly a full year, making harp seals strictly seasonal breeders with a single pup born annually.

Sexual maturation in harp seals is a protracted process relative to their relatively short lactation period. The time elapsed since birth at puberty is approximately 2,190 days [tp = approximately 2,190 days], which equates to roughly six years of age for individua at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]ls in the wild. This developmental milestone, measured at the standard body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], coincides with the attainment of a standard length at puberty of about 137 centimeters [Lp = about 137 centimeters]. Puberty in males is often delayed by an additional one to two years compared to females, a pattern common among polygynous pinnipeds. The onset of gonadal activity is linked to the achievement of a critical body size rather than age alone, as slower-growing individuals may postpone maturation. Field studies in the Barents Sea and off Newfoundland indicate that females typically become reproductively mature at a slightly smaller body length than males, though the population-level average remains near 137 cm. After reaching sexual maturity, females enter a reproductive cycle that may continue for several decades.

The maximum lifespan of the harp seal is considerable for a mammal of its body size, with individuals documented to survive for more than 30 years in the wild. This estimated life span of approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] is recorded at a standard core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The species' reproductive output is regulated by the fact that females typically produce a single pup each year once sexually mature, yielding a maximum reproductive rate of one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year]. This annual single-pup strategy, when combined with a potential reproductive lifespan of over two decades, results in a lifetime litter production of perhaps 20 to 25 pups under optimal conditions. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult harp seal is around 180,000 grams [Wwi = around 180,000 grams], a mass that reflects the extensive blubber layer essential for thermoregulation and energy storage. Adult males tend to be slightly larger and heavier than females, though the dimorphism is modest compared to other phocid species such as elephant seals.
